_about.what: The numbers of a fleet action fought out on the field (src/battle/sea). Every ship's weight, toughness and nation's quality come from data/campaign/navy.json, as the rules count them: this file only says how the field plays them out. Abstract by design (project memory air-battle-paused, ruling 217): pieces wear each other down within reach, by the angle their guns bear; nothing is aimed and nothing flies.
_about.field: The sea is a square of 'size' metres. The attacker's fleets come on from the south edge, 'edge' metres in, the defender's from the north, in rows 'row' metres apart: destroyers ahead, then cruisers, battleships and carriers. 'limit' is the battle time in seconds before it is called on the exchange so far.
_about.classes: speed in metres a second at cruising speed (the historian's: battleships 11, cruisers 13, destroyers 14, carriers 13); turn in radians a second at full way (a ship turns slower when slow, and barely at all when stopped); reach is the furthest its guns hit at all (the one ring the screens draw) and a ship nearer the enemy than three quarters of best turns away to open the range; per is how many ships of the class sail as one piece (destroyers in fours); crew is a ship's company, for the after-action card only; len and beam are a ship's length and breadth in metres, for the screens and the 3D models; a piece's ships sail in line ahead, three lengths apart. Battleships, cruisers and destroyers have one reach and hit with one punch for each unit of their weight (the design director, b415, upheld by ruling 239): the campaign's card already prices a battleship as more weight than a cruiser, so the field does not count the class a second time. Reach by class was measured and withdrawn: reach is worth weight (the longer reach lands its weight first, and early harm compounds), and the card prices weight, not reach. A destroyer's smaller guns are left to the look. Classes differ in speed, turning, toughness and their place in the line, and their salvos differ in look only (battleships slow and heavy, destroyers quick and light: SALVO in src/battle/ui/sea-draw.ts), with the same harm per unit of weight each minute. A carrier fights by its strike, not its guns: standoff is how far it keeps from the nearest enemy, behind its own screen and beyond the guns' reach.
_about.speeds: Shares of a class's cruising speed for the speed order, and accel, how fast way is gained or lost (metres a second, each second).
_about.fire: rate turns weight into wear on a hull each second, the same for every class. hull: a side's hulls together come to this many times its weight, shared over its ships by the rules' toughness (a battleship takes about twice the wear of its weight that a destroyer does); every shot, strike and raid takes the same weight out of the fight whatever ship it falls on, so toughness decides which ships go down and not who wins. far is what a piece does at the edge of its reach against 1 at its best range or closer: 1, so guns tell as hard anywhere in reach, and a ship in the rear rows is not worth less than its weight for standing further back (at 0.5, a fleet strong in the ships behind the line won 10 points less than the card). endOn is what its guns do when the target is dead ahead or astern, against 1 on the beam: crossing the T. damaged: a crippled ship still fights at this share. retarget: seconds between a piece looking for a new target.
_about.nerve: A piece's nerve falls by 'hit' for each whole hull it takes in wear, and when a ship of its own side goes down within 'nearR' metres by 'near' times that ship's share of its side's weight (a cruiser lost from a fleet of weight 60 shakes it by 0.06, a destroyer by 0.02, a battleship by 0.2: the design director, b438), so a fleet of many light ships is shaken no more for the same weight lost; out of the fight for 'quiet' seconds it mends at 'mend' a second. Below 'waver' it wavers and fights at 'wavering'; below 'break' it breaks off for its own edge.
_about.side: A side breaks off when it has lost 'breakAt' of its strength as the card counts it, its ships and its coasts' aircraft together (a share of 'spread' either way, more with a good admiral: 'admiral' a level). After a side breaks, its enemy has 'pursuit' seconds to make it pay before the battle ends. The luck of the day is the rules' own: one roll of the dice's run (0.8 to 1.2, navy.ts seaBattles) for the battle, the attacker's ships fighting that much better and the defender's that much worse, so that with nobody playing the field gives what the dice give. Once the enemy has broken off, every ship of the side still fighting runs it down at full speed, the player's as the staff's, until the player gives an order of their own (b402). An order from the chasing side to hold, to break off or to steer for a point lets the beaten enemy go: the action ends there, the side that broke off beaten and the losses as they stand (b458). An order to attack it is a pursuit, and the chase runs on. A ship still afloat at the end with 'hurt' of its hull or less left, or gone out of the fight burning, came home badly hurt: the after card names it by its kind, the enemy's as the player's, so a victory over a fleet that took its wrecks home reads as one (b458). A ship worn to 'hurt' of her own hull or less leaves the line burning and makes for port, whether she sinks the dice's limit by class; the side whose blow put her out owes the hull she takes with her, paid out of its next blows, and it counts toward her side's loss only as it is paid: what is unpaid at the end counts on neither side (the ship plan's R2). A ship breaking off steers away from the enemy nearest her still fighting, bent for home (the sum of the two directions), so she opens the range as she goes; by the field's side edges she holds for home (R5).
_about.strike: A carrier's strike: ordered, it is flown within the second and lands 'windup' seconds later on the target and the ships near it within 'radius', and the carrier can strike again 'every' seconds after that. A strike carries the weight of 'every' seconds of the carrier's own weight at 'share', its own weight being what is left of its air group. It takes the same weight out of the fight whatever ship it falls on (wear in proportion to the ship's hull), so the screen is no cheaper a target than the battleship. Every blow on a side, by gun, strike or raid, wears the whole of what the side brought by weight: the ship it fell on for the gun ships' share, each carrier for its own (as a hull wears, but out of its air group: it stays afloat) and the coasts' aircraft for theirs (b415). Kept whole at 6,000 m while the gun ships wore, carriers were worth more the longer the gun fight ran, a tenth or more of the card either way with the fleets' make-up; worn with their fleet, share 0.34 keeps them within the dice attacking and attacked, with a light screen or a mixed one. Carriers with no gun ship at all are not: the field cannot honour an action where one side has none, so the staff settles it and the field is not offered it (the design director, b438: carriers against carriers is an air battle, and the field flies no planes). With no strike ordered, or under a fleet order, a carrier strikes by its job (jobs.strike): the enemy's carriers first, then battleships, cruisers and destroyers, the one nearest its fleet's main effort; where its style shares fire out (spread), a second carrier takes a second enemy carrier before doubling up. A strike ordered on one piece goes where it is sent. Hit the flight decks first, then the battleships (the panel's principle; Midway, June 1942). Once a side has broken off, no carrier flies a new strike unless the player has sent it after the beaten enemy since (b458): the staff's carriers, and a carrier left to itself, let the enemy go. It is counted, not flown: no aircraft are on the field, and a strike in the air does not slow the screens' fast approach, which runs until the guns meet (b458).
_about.air: Aircraft from the coasts (the rules' airOver, times navy.json air.weight) raid every 'every' seconds, the first within the first raid's span; each raid's weight is 'share' of what that much weight of guns would deal in the time, as a strike's is, and like gunfire it takes the same weight out of the fight whatever ship it finds. A raid finds its ship by the campaign's own aim (carriers.json strike.aim, read only: carriers 3, battleships 2, cruisers 1, destroyers 0.5), times the ships afloat in each piece, with one draw as before. The card counts the coasts' aircraft in a side's strength, so the field does: they are worn by every blow on their side by their share of its weight, and having no hull they lose the whole of it, where a ship's hull takes it at 'fire.hull' (b415). Each raid is as strong as the aircraft left. Share 0.55 keeps the coasts' aircraft within the dice on either side, from a few against a fleet to most of a side's strength. It was 0.5 until every class drew up on one front (b458, see pieces): a gun fleet's whole weight then came to bear, and a fleet of 16 ships won 62 and 65 in 100 at even odds, attacking and attacked, against 8 destroyers whose side was four fifths aircraft. At 0.55 it wins 47 either way, and at 0.6, 31 and 36.
_about.pieces: No more than 'most' pieces a side: past that, cruisers sail in twos, then destroyers in more than fours. Every class's row is 'front' metres times its share of its side's weight, the same metres for every class, with its pieces spaced evenly along it: a row of battleships, carriers, cruisers or destroyers that carries a third of its side's weight is a third of 3,250 m wide. So two fleets of the same weight meet on the same front whatever their make and however many pieces they come in (b438, b458). 'front' replaced 'frontage' (the design director, b458), which spaced each class at its own natural gap (650 m between big ships, 500 m between fours of destroyers, at a side's weight of 50), so that each unit of a side's weight stood on 3,250 m of front in a battleship row, 4,643 m in a carrier row, 6,250 m in a destroyer row and 10,833 m in a cruiser row. A light line then stood two or three times as wide as a battle line of the same weight, its wings out of reach: 12 cruisers and 12 destroyers won 31 in 100 against 3 battleships, 2 cruisers and 8 destroyers at even odds, and 'Carriers against a battle line' won 66 against a card of 71. On one front they win 45 and 70. 3,250 m keeps a battleship row as wide as it was. At 2,500 m the largest fleets fell further from the card, and at 3,600 m or more a fleet of 23 pieces lost 97 in 100 at even odds to one of 18 of much the same make.
_about.ai: The computer's captains (and the player's, where no order is given): each side has a main effort, the enemy piece nearest the middle of its own fleet, kept until it goes or breaks off, when the enemy then nearest the middle that is still fighting takes its place. Around it each ship does its class's job ('jobs'). That is exactly what a newcomer does (select all, right-click the enemy nearest the middle, Space): an order to attack given to two or more pieces is a fleet order, which sets the main effort and leaves each piece to its job, so the newcomer's battle and the staff's are the same (b402, ruling 239). An order to one piece alone is its own target. A ship further than 'keep' metres from the middle of its own fleet works back toward it as it fights. A ship steers for the enemy nearest it, and for the main effort only when that lies more than 'beyond' metres further off than the nearest enemy (ruling 226, 4: every ship sent at one point made a knot the enemy fought around). Until the guns first meet, a fleet keeps together: its gun ships sail at the speed of its slowest gun ship, and one more than 'station' metres ahead of the rearmost of them slows to half that speed until the line comes up, so the screen closes up on the battle line and stays just ahead of it (the historian: fleet speed was the slowest heavy ship's, and the screen kept station on the battle line). Drawn up 700 m a row apart and each at its own speed, a battle line reached the fight a minute after its screen and lost to a light fleet of the same weight 95 times in 100; with the screen kept 600 m ahead it still came 13 in 100 short (b407, ruling 217). A fleet keeps together only to meet a gun line: not once either side has broken off (the chase runs at full speed) and not against an enemy with no gun ship left: then every gun ship not sent at a speed of its own runs the carriers down at full speed, as a broken enemy is. While it keeps together a fleet also holds one course, from its own middle to the enemy's, so the line comes on as it drew up: each steering for the enemy nearest it, the wings turned in toward the middle and the line came on bunched (b438). A ship the player sends at a speed of their own, or on a course, goes as told, and a destroyer piece whose torpedo run has opened goes in at flank (torp; the ship plan's R4). A ship within 'broadside' metres of the enemy it is steering for turns to bring its broadside to bear; further off it closes. Closing until 3,450 m left the ships behind their own screen end-on for the whole fight. The AA ring (the ship plan's R3; the design director, 14:36Z): while the enemy brings aircraft and until the guns first meet, a side with carriers and no battleship keeps its whole escort, cruisers and destroyers at cruising speed fighting at will or under a fleet order and not on a torpedo run, round its carriers at torp's 'station' metres (inside the strike's radius, so their guns count against aircraft and they share what a strike lands), spaced evenly round from the bearing of the enemy's middle, the pieces shared in turn over the carriers fighting at will or sent to strike. At contact they fight as any other ship does. Held through the action the ring kept its guns' weight out of the fight, which the card prices whole: carriers against carriers missed the card by .13 to .38 in every such form, and the campaign's flak law hands back 0.2 to 0.3% of a strike whatever the ring. It is let go for good once a carrier of its side sights an enemy battleship within evade's 'see' metres: the screen left the carriers to meet surface ships (Samar, October 1944), and a ring that turned away with them kept the guns from meeting for most of the action, or all of it. None once a side has broken off, or against an enemy with no gun ship left. While the enemy brings aircraft a carrier keeps station 'keep' metres astern of the middle of its gun ships keeping with the fleet (not those in the ring, on a run, or sent at a target, a speed or a course of the player's own), on the line from the enemy's middle through theirs, and further back until no enemy lies within its standoff (the 1944 War Instructions: carrier groups manoeuvre away from the enemy); kept inside the field's edge by the margin of the turn away, which may bring it nearer. Two or more stand abreast across that line, their navy's spacing apart ('carriers': the record's one figure for carriers in one group, whatever they stand behind; it was torp's 'station', 1,000 m, closer than any figure in the record: the design director, 21:00Z). On station it keeps the gun ships' course and way, never below its slow speed. With no such gun ship (a carrier group whose escorts are all in its ring) it keeps its standoff as before, and a carrier the player sends at a speed of their own goes as told. Once the guns have met the station runs only while the side has a battleship afloat and not breaking off, its carriers astern of the line (Formidable stayed out on the disengaged side at Matapan while the battleships fought); a carrier group has none after contact, the ring's window: it is the screen's geometry, so it runs when the screen does (kept on, it held the group's carriers astern through the gun fight and the cruiser-heavy side lost .05 more of the card). With no station, two or more carriers keep their navy's way ('carriers', by navy and era: the design director, 20:50Z): each for herself, never inside the navy's spacing of a sister, or on a guide, the first by id keeping her standoff at a pace her followers can close on and each other her place abreast of her; a carrier with an enemy strike aloft at her leaves the guide's formation and steers on her own, never inside the spacing of a sister (let each steer off her own nearest enemy with neither, a carrier group's carriers came 132-214 m apart in the gun fight). Its turn into the wind to launch is the 3D game's to show: the rules keep its course.
_about.evade: A carrier group without battleships that sees an enemy battleship within 'see' metres of a carrier turns away from it and opens the range at 'speed' times a carrier's cruising speed, launching as it goes, unless the player has ordered it to steer, hold or withdraw (a carrier evades even when ordered to strike). Near the edge of the field it turns along it. 'screen' is how near a carrier a ship of its screen must be to turn away with it: 0, so the screen stays and fights (b402: a screen that ran with its carriers left the plain order short of the card). A fleet with battleships of its own stands and fights, its carriers behind the line. Before the guns first meet, where the enemy brings aircraft, a carrier group's escorts keep the AA ring round its carriers (ai), and the ring is let go the moment a carrier sights a battle line: the screen stays and fights as b402 has it (the ship plan's R3).
_about.jobs: Each ship class to its own job (the tactics panel's item 2, ruling 239): 'fire' lists, for each gun class, the enemy classes it fires on, in order; 'strike', the enemy classes a carrier strikes, in order (see strike). A piece takes the first class it has in reach, ships still fighting before ships breaking off, and among them the one nearest its fleet's main effort; a style that shares the big guns' fire out ('spread' 1) has each battleship and cruiser take, among them, the one fewest of its side's battleships and cruisers are firing on (ties: nearest the main effort, then its own left), and keep it until another has two fewer. So big guns go on big ships and no enemy big ship is left untroubled, cruisers fight cruisers and back the line, and destroyers fight destroyers and cruisers, turning their guns on battleships and carriers only when nothing else is in reach: a destroyer's shells burst on a big ship's upper works and never pierced its belt (Samar, October 1944; Hiei, November 1942), and its real blow at a big ship is the torpedo run (torp). A bar on destroyer guns firing at big ships was measured and withdrawn (ruling 239): it held priced weight out of the fight. No dice: the same ships in the same places make the same choice. The navies shared fire so that no enemy capital ship went unengaged, and cruisers engaged cruisers (the panel's history notes).
_about.torp: The destroyers' torpedo run (the tactics panel's item 3, ruling 239). A destroyer piece whose guns have nothing in reach banks their weight each second after the guns first meet (fire's rate times its weight, its nerve and the day, with no range or angle), up to 'bank' seconds' worth, and that bank is its salvo: weight its guns could not fire, so the card's weight is moved, not added to. On a run its guns keep firing at whatever their job finds in reach, so a run takes no weight out of the fight. A run: on the cues below, a steady destroyer piece outside the screen goes for the enemy big ship nearest the main effort within 'start' metres, battleships first, then cruisers, then carriers; with spread 1 the ship fewest runs are closing on first (pieces opening together still go as one division at one target). A piece runs only with a full salvo banked ('bank' seconds' worth at its guns' weight now); short of one it chases with its guns, as destroyers that had fired off their torpedoes did (the ship plan's R5). It goes in with its tubes full: a full salvo loaded at the start, drawn in advance from its guns' later fire. Weight its guns cannot fire earns it down, and on a run that includes what its guns lose bearing end-on going in and stern-on coming out, which pays its own salvo's advance first, before and after it launches, the rest banking as ever (the design director, 08:10Z: the bank is the weight the guns could not fire, so the run's lost gunfire is not a second cost on top of the advance); what is still unearned when the salvo lands is owed by its side then, paid out of the side's gunfire weight for weight, as R2's debt is paid out of its blows, and like that debt it counts on neither side until it is paid (the break and the odds read weight dealt: the design director, 09:48Z), so a loaded salvo never fired, or still running when the action ends, moves no weight; once fired, the tubes fill again only by the bank (the design director, 05:01Z and 06:14Z: owed at launch out of the destroyer's own guns, it was paid in the deciding minutes for weight that lands after the break, since as the run's clock then stood no salvo landed before it). It closes at flank, launches at its style's 'press' range (a cover run, on the Samar cue below, as soon as its target is within 'start' metres: its job is to turn her away, and at Samar Johnston fired at about 9,000 m and the others soon after: the design director, 11:25Z), turns away at flank for 'away' seconds and rejoins; it may run again 'again' seconds after it launched. Wavering on the run-in breaks it off, its bank kept for the next. The salvo runs 'travel' seconds and falls on its target, as any blow does (the same weight out of the fight whatever it falls on); with the target gone, on the enemy nearest where it was aimed within 'radius' metres, else on the heaviest. When a run goes is what its crews could see, never a clock (the ship plan's R4; the design director, 06:14Z and 06:48Z). A piece's run opens at once, at the ship doing the threatening within 'start' metres, ahead of her beam or not, when an enemy battleship or cruiser is coming at one of the side's carriers, heading at her (she lies ahead of its beam), the range falling, and making more way than she does, so it will overtake her (a carrier keeping her distance is the very flight the screen covers), or is within its own gun reach of one of the side's battleships where the enemy's heavy ships in reach of her outnumber the side's own in reach of them (Samar, October 1944: the escort carriers' screen ran early as Kurita's ships came on and turned them away), and such a division launches at once and runs on through its own side's break, covering the withdrawal; at once, once the guns have met and while a battleship or cruiser of its own side is within gun reach of an enemy battleship or cruiser (one still fighting, or one it is running down once the enemy has broken off), when it lies ahead of the beam of the enemy big ship it would run at, within 'start' metres (of the course she flees on, for a ship running for home: a piece on her bow as she turns away is soon astern of her) (the record's firing position ahead of the target's beam; by day the record's runs at an alert line came while the lines were engaged, at Jutland, the Java Sea and North Cape, and unsupported destroyers ran in at a heavy line only to cover something, so a destroyer-only side opens none; Surigao's runs before the guns met were the night's, which the field does not fight: the design director, 08:10Z and 09:48Z); and, abaft her beam, once its style's torpWhen finds the enemy's big ships in reach of the side's big guns shaken to that much of their nerve, slowed by gunfire (North Cape, December 1943). The pieces whose runs open in the same second go as one division at one target, the one the piece nearest its own target would take (a ship threatening the side's carriers or outnumbered battleships first), those of them within 'start' metres of her (the others open their own in the next second): they close in company, a piece more than the fleet's station distance (ai.station) nearer the target than the division's rearmost slowing to half until it comes up, and each launches at press, so the division's salvoes land together (a cover division launches at once, its target being in reach). Sea visibility and night actions are not modelled yet (on the after-release list, from the battle's one weather draw). The screen (styles: screen) is the destroyer pieces nearest the side's big ships as it draws up: each keeps 'station' metres ahead of the big ship it guards, toward the enemy, until its guns find a target, and then fights where it is, as the line's other pieces do (held on station, its weight stood out of the fight); it steers for any enemy run within 'intercept' metres and fires first on destroyers making a run; it never runs, and launches its bank from station at an enemy big ship that comes within press. A fleet with no big ship keeps no screen. Once no enemy destroyer is afloat its job is done, and its pieces run and fight as any other destroyer does (the design director, 22:57Z). Destroyers screened the line and attacked in groups with torpedoes, then turned away (North Cape, December 1943; Samar, October 1944: the panel's history notes). A battleship, cruiser or carrier with tracks running at her combs them (the ship plan's R6; the design director, 05:17Z): the ship a salvo is fired at, and every battleship, cruiser or carrier of her side within 'radius' metres of its aim point (its water), turns away from the tick after the launch, her stern to the tracks on their bearing from the launcher's place to the aim point, the shorter way round (to starboard with them dead at her bow), until the salvo lands ('travel'), as the record's ships turned away from tracks running at them whether or not aimed at them (Jutland, 31 May 1916: Hercules, Revenge, Colossus, from tracks fired at the line; Samar, 25 October 1944: Yamato, from torpedoes that missed Haruna), while the hit is unchanged: the salvo still lands on the ship it was fired at with its whole weight, wherever she steers. What her guns cannot bring to bear while she combs is banked, as a destroyer's idle guns' weight is, and goes with her first blow once the comb is over, on the ship her guns bear on, and no more: the bank is the weight the guns could not fire, every class and every navy (the design director, 11:58Z) (while the rule is built in steps, the water and a carrier group's ships wait their step). Release 2's own water, only with the campaign's switch on (the options page's 'Friendly torpedoes'; Brian, 25 November 12:52Z: friendly ships passed right in front of their own side's torpedoes): a salvo's water is the fan from the launcher's place at the launch, as wide there as her beam, to 'radius' metres either side of its aim point, its heads crossing it in 'travel' seconds; a piece's ships are where the 3D game lays them, her leader at the piece's place and the rest astern of him along the way he came, three lengths apart. A destroyer piece holds its salvo while another ship of its side, on her course and way, would be in that water as the heads come level with her, and launches the first second the way is clear: on a run it keeps closing at flank meanwhile, and from the screen's station it looks again each second. Every ship of the side with way on, of every class and whatever she is doing, that the heads of a salvo of her side's (not her own) would pass through turns square off its tracks, on the side of them she lies, from the tick after its launch until the heads are past her or it lands, at her own speed; a comb of an enemy salvo stands and the field's edge wins. The crews' rule in the record: a ship of one's own in the line of fire fouled the range and the tubes waited, and ships kept clear of their own side's torpedo water. Off, the field is as before to the byte. Geometry of the field's own numbers: no new number, no dice.
_about.styles: How a side's captains fight (ruling 239): a temperament, not a weapon. The card has priced the fight, so a style changes how the action unfolds, never how much weight each side brings. 'spread': 1 shares the big guns' fire out over the enemy's big ships (jobs), 0 fires on the one nearest the main effort. 'torpWhen': a destroyer piece abaft the beam of its target opens its run once the enemy big ships in the big guns' reach average this much of their nerve or less (1, at first contact); runs ahead of the beam, or against a ship threatening the side's carriers or outnumbered battleships, open at once (torp). 'press': the range a run closes to before it launches, in metres (a cover run launches once its target is within torp.start: torp). 'screen': the share of the side's destroyer pieces kept back as the screen, rounded down, and at least one where the share is above 0 and there are two or more. 'cover': the share of each carrier strike held back as fighters over the fleet when the enemy brings aircraft (cap); a strike the player orders holds back the same share (ruling 239, 12).
_about.cap: Fighters and guns over the fleet (ruling 239; the tactics panel's item 3, at sea): two neutral trades, so they move where weight falls, never how much. Fighters: when the enemy brings aircraft (a carrier with its air group, or the coasts' aircraft), each carrier flies (1 - cover) of its strike and holds the rest over the fleet, its side's pool; what it holds and has not spent flies with its next strike, so nothing is lost. A strike or a raid of weight W coming in is met by the pool and denied min(pool, W x cap.spoil x the square root of pool / (pool + W)): cap.spoil is the campaign's own (carriers.json cap.spoil, 0.8; air.ts), and the pool pays what it denies, weight for weight, out of each carrier's cover by its share. Guns: the gun ships within the strike's radius of the ship it finds deny f of what is left, f the sum of their ships times carriers.json flak.ships times flak.per, to at most flak.most (0.12), the campaign's own law; each ship pays its share, weight for weight, out of its own next gunfire, and a ship that leaves the fight hands what it owes to the nearest of its side still fighting. Both are told as events, 'sea:cap' (the share the fighters denied) and 'sea:flak' (what the guns denied), for the 3D game: fighters circling over the fleet, flak over the screen.
_about.carrierBattle: Where both sides bring carriers and neither a battleship (ruling 239, 11): 'field' fights it out here, carriers striking from beyond the guns' reach; 'staff' leaves it to the dice, as an action where one side has no gun ship is (b438). It stays 'field' until the design director has read how many such actions the campaign fights.
_about.look: What the 3D game draws and nothing in the rules reads (the ship plan's B1, ruling 239 at 23:20Z: look fields that move no number, src/battle/sea/sim.ts showLooks). A ship that goes out of the fight burning limps for her own side's edge, her course turned off it by up to half of 'limpSpread' radians either way (a hash of her piece and how many it has lost, no dice), at 'limpSpeed' of her class's cruising speed, in place of the 3D game freezing her where she left the line.
_about.line: The battle line (the ship plan's R1, ruling 239's order at 23:20Z; src/battle/sea/sim.ts planLines). Once the guns have met, each side's battleships and cruisers fighting at will or under a fleet order turn together onto one course and keep it at the cruising speed of the slowest of them: the rows they drew up in become columns in line ahead, as long as the rows were wide (b438), the foremost along the course the van. The course is square to the bearing of the enemy's line (its battleships and cruisers), bent toward it by up to 'bend' radians while it lies beyond best range (at the guns' reach, the whole of it) and away while within it, so the rear row comes into reach; on the hand the enemy's line is moving across that bearing (more than 'across' metres a second on average), so the line keeps level with its van and bends across its head as it draws ahead, crossing its T. With the enemy coming straight on it turns to starboard, as the enemy's captains do: the field is the same turned half round for either side (b402), so the lines pass on opposite courses and wheel to keep each other abeam. Turning toward the field's east instead put the defender's line ahead of the attacker's and won it 3 to 5 in 100 more of the same fleets. It turns together onto the other hand when its van's course would take it within 'margin' metres of the field's edge 'edge' metres on, and when its van steers within 'crossed' radians of an enemy line whose course lies square to the bearing (its T crossed: it turns away together onto the hand that runs with the enemy); once formed, and after a turn together, it holds its hand 'settle' seconds while it comes round. A piece more than ai.keep metres from the middle of the line works back toward it at up to flank. There is no line against destroyers alone: at the speed of its slowest ship a line could not bring them to action, and against coasts' aircraft the gun fleet lost 7 in 100 more than the card either way round. A carrier group without battleships forms none: its cruisers stay with its carriers (the historian: Samar, October 1944), and in line they lost the carriers' side 6 to 9 in 100 to a battle line. A piece the player sends at a target, a point or a speed of its own leaves the line; it dissolves once a side breaks off or the enemy has no gun ship left, and the chase is run as before. Destroyers keep their jobs (torp). No dice. Fought each ship for itself, broadside on at the edge of reach, a line's rear row stood out of reach (bbl: the battleships idle 0.86 a battle and losing 0.69 to angle and range).
_about.carriers: How a navy's carriers keep company where they keep no station (the design director, 20:50Z and 20:56Z, by navy and era as a 239 style; the historian's carrier-spacing-record.md); where they keep station (ai) they stand abreast at the same spacing (21:00Z). Each navy has a path, '_' every navy not named; a side stands at the step its research has reached, one step for each of 'grow' it holds in order (the campaign's Carrier task forces: 'fast carriers, battleships and their screen sailing and fighting as one body'), read off the nation's record by the sea ticket as land's styles grow by doctrines held, never by a date. 'herself': each carrier steers off her own enemy, but never closes inside 'spacing' metres of a sister: with one inside it and her course closing on her she turns square to the line between them, neither closing nor opening by will (every navy in 1942 and Japan throughout manoeuvred each for herself under air attack and drew apart by miles: Coral Sea, Midway). 'guide': the first carrier by id in formation is the guide and keeps her standoff, at slow while a follower lies more than 'spacing' metres from her place, so they reach their places; each other keeps her place abreast of the guide, 'spacing' metres apart across the line from the enemy (the US cruising dispositions from late 1943; the British Pacific Fleet, 1945, on US signal books). Both run wherever the carriers keep no station, before the guns meet as after (a carrier group's ring holds every gun ship, so it has no station before contact either). A carrier with an enemy strike aloft at her is out of the guide's formation and steers her own standoff, as a carrier under direct attack swung on her own, and a guide under attack hands the formation to the next by id; the spacing line binds her still (with none under attack, two carriers struck at once came 9-80 m apart). The spacings are the record's laid figures: US 1942 2,740 m (Coral Sea, 3,000 yd, H), US late 1943-45 and the BPF about 2,300 m (2,500 yd, L-M), Japan's Kido Butai box 7,000 m (M), Formation ZK 2,000 m (1944, L, inferred); Britain 1942 has no figure and takes the US 1942 one; a navy not named takes the US path, the guide coming with the research. Not laid: the US June 1942 to mid-1943 step of one carrier to a ring, the rings 9,000-18,500 m apart, which nothing on the ticket marks (the design director, 20:56Z: no marker invented).
